permitted_claims.statement: The bounded primary-text shortlist is fixed to four cases: administrative tablet P005390/MMA 1988.433.2, private letter MMA 86.11.111, lexical school tablet P228744, and literary composition ETCSL 3.1.19.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: The four cases cover distinct functional turns but cannot represent every city, period, social group or genre.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only these four handoff candidates unless a later production task documents why a substitution is needed.

permitted_claims.statement: MMA 86.11.111 is a ca. 1632 BCE Old Babylonian letter in which Marduk-mushallim reports failure to implement a royal security order.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Its probable Sippar-Yahrurum origin lacks excavated context, and the museum itself presents the letter as unusual.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use as an exceptional human-scale epistolary case illustrating reporting and command, not as representative everyday correspondence or proof that writing caused compliance.

permitted_claims.statement: A written law, norm or transaction is evidence of recording and claim-making, not automatic evidence of enforcement.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Case-specific links among tablet, witnesses, seal and action are required.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: Agency belongs to people and institutions using records: tablets stabilize classifications, scribes and sealers authenticate them, archives make them retrievable, and authorities supply enforcement.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: The strength of each link differs by archive; a preserved record alone cannot demonstrate enforcement.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Never say writing itself commanded, owned or coerced.
